title: Musical assessment of the Burley session
summary: Rose praises Burley's earthy Harlem sound and Pops Foster's bass, and says the session taught him he could only make records following his own musical views.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Well, what, what did you think of the music as far as that's concerned? The Burley?
Oh, well, uh, it was pretty interesting. Of course, I was very fond of Dan's playing all the time.

It was a very earthy sound, and, uh, and, uh, extremely indigenous to the, at that time, to the Harlem scene. And, uh, of course, I was always overwhelmed by Pops Foster's bass playing. Yeah. Yeah. And, um, I thought that the rhythm was excellent. Of course, I would not make a record like that today, because I more or less, uh, let Dan have his head in that, and Dan was partial to this saxophone player, John Hardy, who played on a session. Well, played on a session. And I suppose that he was a very good saxophone player, but I discovered, uh, in making that session, that I wasn't really going to be able to make anything successfully that, uh, wasn't actually following out my own musical views. Although, I considered that to be a, uh, an interesting session. Yeah. Looks like you're running out of tape. Yeah, that's what I was just noticing.
